builder_plan.scenario: Your self-hosted model spends too long generating answers token by token.
builder_plan.change: Check whether a compatible draft model and serving integration exist before renting compute.
builder_plan.baseline: The same target with speculation off, then your existing drafter if you have one.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Accepted draft length, tokens per second, tail latency, output quality, and total GPU cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Look Back, Draft Ahead: Corrective Prefix Attention for Parallel Speculative Decoding
summary: CPA replaces existing parallel speculative drafters (DSpark, DFlash) by letting block candidates attend to earlier in-block choices via precomputed pairwise interaction tables, avoiding repeated neural evaluations during the sequential selection walk. Its cost is an additional training phase: the shared backbone must be fine-tuned with an auxiliary autoregressive loss on clean prefixes, plus implementation complexity for the shortlist tables, though inference adds no extra forward pass. Failure modes include gains that do not transfer beyond the reported math, code, and dialogue workloads, results measured only on Ascend NPUs with Qwen3-4B/8B, the authors' own finding that higher acceptance does not guarantee faster decoding, and possible unavailability of portable open-source implementations.
rationale: The acceptance-rate and speedup gains over existing parallel drafters are meaningful for latency-bound inference on a single GPU, but the method requires fine-tuning the target backbone with an auxiliary autoregressive loss, so the reader must validate training cost, reproducibility, and absence of vendor-specific (Ascend NPU) dependencies before committing.
technique: Corrective Prefix Attention for parallel speculative decoding

claims.statement: CPA replaces existing parallel speculative drafters (DSpark, DFlash) by letting block candidates attend to earlier in-block choices via precomputed pairwise interaction tables, avoiding repeated neural evaluations during the sequential selection walk. Its cost is an additional training phase: the shared backbone must be fine-tuned with an auxiliary autoregressive loss on clean prefixes, plus implementation complexity for the shortlist tables, though inference adds no extra forward pass. Failure modes include gains that do not transfer beyond the reported math, code, and dialogue workloads, results measured only on Ascend NPUs with Qwen3-4B/8B, the authors' own finding that higher acceptance does not guarantee faster decoding, and possible unavailability of portable open-source implementations.

CPA commits 13–15% more tokens per verification round than DSpark and 25–26% more than DFlash, reaching mean speedups of 3.35× and 3.37× under greedy decoding and 2.86× under sampling on Qwen3-4B/8B targets.
